Why Leon Homes Need Quality Roofing

Leon's climate punishes roofs in ways that casual observers might miss. With 33 inches of annual rainfall and 12 inches of snow, water intrusion becomes a constant threat when roofing systems start to fail. The 76 freeze days each year create expansion and contraction cycles, but it's the 37 freeze-thaw cycles that cause the real damage—water seeps into tiny cracks, freezes overnight, expands, and splits shingles apart from the inside.

The National Weather Service monitors Butler County through their ICT office using KICT radar, and their data tells a story Leon homeowners know well: severe storms dominate the disaster history here. Those 99 severe storm declarations over the last ten years mean high winds, hail, and driving rain that strip granules, lift shingles, and compromise flashing. One fire event rounds out the disaster profile, but it's the relentless storm activity that keeps roofing contractors busy.

Temperature swings between an average high of 68°F and an average low of 49°F might seem mild, but they create constant stress on roofing materials. The West Branch Walnut River near El Dorado currently shows very low flow, but Leon sits in FEMA Flood Zone X—minimal flood risk outside the 500-year floodplain. That's good news for foundation concerns, but it doesn't protect roofs from the weather coming from above.

With a median household income of $67,500, Leon families make thoughtful decisions about home improvements. They recognize that quality roofing protects everything beneath it, from family heirlooms to the structure itself.
